method: Wikimedia Commons API (action=query, prop=imageinfo, iiprop=extmetadata) for verbatim license/author metadata; all 23 download URLs (12 heroes + 11 alternates) live-checked via HEAD request, all HTTP 200; identity cross-checked against data/case-records/*.json and registry-unified.json; reverse-geocoded author-supplied GPS coordinates via OpenStreetMap Nominatim where available (Pittston, Gary, Delhi); visually inspected full-resolution images for exterior/interior and hero selection; targeted web searches (Greater Pittston Historical Society, WNEP) to resolve two building-identity questions (Pittston, Wilkes-Barre) where the 1899 album photo appears to predate a later building replacement/rebuild documented for the parish.

verified.author: Jonas Žilius (writing under pseudonym "Jonas, Jr.")
verified.licenseVerbatim: Commons LicenseShortName: "Public domain"; UsageTerms: "Public domain"; permission template {{PD-old-70-1923}}. Credit line: "This file is from the Mechanical Curator collection... released to Flickr Commons by the British Library."
verified.identityEvidence: File caption reads "WILKES-BARRE LIETUVISZKA BAŽNYCZIA" ("Wilkes-Barre's Lithuanian church"); Commons notes field: "The Catholic Church of lithuanian emigrants in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania." Wilkes-Barre had exactly one Lithuanian parish, Holy Trinity (Švč. Trejybės), at 416 E. South Street, matching case-record data/case-records/svc-trejybes-wilkes-barre-pa.json. Image extracted from page 91 of 'Lietuviai Amerikoj' (1899) by Jonas Žilius, British Library HMNTS 10412.ee.38, digitized via British Library/Flickr Commons Mechanical Curator project.
verified.verdict: accept - hero (only known image; historic PD scan). CORRECTION: task brief cited this as from an 1898 'Lietuviszkas albumas' — the Commons record instead documents it as page 91 of 'Lietuviai Amerikoj' (Lithuanians in America), published 1899 by Jonas Žilius under the pseudonym 'Jonas, Jr.' (a real, separate 1898 book titled 'Lietuviszkas albumas' also exists on Commons under different file names/IDs, e.g. 'Lietuviszkas albumas - Lithuanian album 1898 (191...).jpg', but it is NOT the source of this specific file). Use 'Lietuviai Amerikoj (1899), by Jonas Žilius' in any caption/credit, not 'Lietuviszkas albumas (1898)'. CAVEAT: 2015 press (WNEP) describes the demolished building as having 'two lofty steeples' dominating the skyline; this 1899 image shows one main tower plus one small secondary cupola on the transept — likely depicts the parish's earlier building phase (pre-dating or predating a possible tower addition/rebuild) rather than the exact final silhouette described in 2015 demolition coverage. Still the same parish/site and the only available image; flagged for editorial awareness, not a rejection.

verified.author: Doug Kerr
verified.licenseVerbatim: Commons LicenseShortName: "CC BY-SA 2.0"; UsageTerms: "Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0"; AttributionRequired: true. Source: Flickr (https://www.flickr.com/photos/7327243@N05/4112069948), uploaded via Flickr upload bot 2011-05-16, reviewed by 'Pauk'. {{cc-by-sa-2.0}} on file page.
verified.identityEvidence: Taken 2009-11-16 (~19 months after the parish's April 6, 2008 closure), geotagged 41.3240282,-75.7874673, which reverse-geocodes to Church Street, Pittston, PA — the Church & Butler Streets corner independently documented by the Greater Pittston Historical Society (greaterpittstonhistory.org) as St. Casimir's exact address. Web research (Greater Pittston Historical Society + general search corroboration) confirms St. Casimir's FINAL building was a 1909 Baroque-style church designed by Louis Giele of New York, built of brick with Indiana limestone trimmings, dedicated Easter Monday March 28, 1910, and used until the 2008 closure — this exactly matches the grand twin-tower, limestone-trimmed, pedimented facade visible in Doug Kerr's photo. The 'Available'/Atlas Realty signage on the building is consistent with the church having just closed and gone up for lease/sale (case-records/sv-kazimiero-pittston-pa.json confirms a 2011 sale to Gina Malsky followed this period). Categorized on Commons under 'Saint Casimir churches in the United States' and 'Churches in Pittston, Pennsylvania.'

alternates.author: Jonas Žilius (pseudonym "Jonas, Jr.")
alternates.note: 1899 image captioned 'PITTSTONO LIETUVISZKA BAŽNYCZIA,' extracted from page 103 of 'Lietuviai Amerikoj' (1899). Shows a modest single-steeple brick chapel — this is almost certainly St. Casimir's FIRST building (parish founded 1885-1890, cornerstone blessed June 30, 1889), which was superseded by the grander 1909 Baroque church shown in the hero image. Same parish, earlier/different building — genuine PD historic image but not the structure that survived to 2008 and stands today as a residence.

verified.verdict: accept - hero is the MODERN Doug Kerr 2009 photo (deviating from the task brief's tentative preference for the 1898/1899 image), because research shows the 1899 scan and the Doug Kerr photo depict two different buildings from two different eras of the same parish, and the Doug Kerr photo depicts the actual 1909-2008 building that survives today as a residential conversion (matching the site's case record). The 1899 image is kept as a historical alternate depicting the parish's earlier chapel, not the surviving building.

Kryžiaus) at Sixth & Poplar Streets has an 1892 Lithuanian cornerstone still in place, and was Mount Carmel's only Lithuanian parish. verified.verdict: accept - hero (only image provided; building still stands per case record, now used as a warehouse — no modern photo available in this pass, but the 1892 date and single building lineage line up cleanly, unlike Wilkes-Barre/Pittston).

Filed under Commons category "St. Casimir Church (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania)." Matches case-records/sv-kazimiero-pittsburgh-pa.json in every particular: South Side Flats, converted 2017-2018 into "22nd Street Condos" at 2132 Sarah Street (case record's cited address; the task brief's '2114 Sarah Street' appears to be a minor transcription variant — both agree on Sarah Street, South Side, the 22nd Street Condos building). Only Lithuanian parish in Pittsburgh (founded 1893, church dedicated 1902). Twin-tower brick Baroque-revival architecture with domed cupolas visible in photo is consistent with the 1902 building.

alternates.author: Cbaile19
alternates.note: 2015-06-15 photo, same building. Author's own file-page note: "This extreme-wide-angle picture of the façade distorts the towers, but otherwise preserves the proportions" — usable but the 2021 photo has no such distortion, hence chosen as hero. 4911x5491px, very high resolution.

alternates.author: Jonas Žilius (pseudonym "Jonas, Jr.")
alternates.note: 1899 image ('Lietuviai Amerikoj' page 169), single-steeple Gothic design — likely depicts the church at or just before its 1902 dedication (3-year gap, plausibly the same building nearing completion, unlike the Wilkes-Barre/Pittston cases where a full later rebuild is documented). NOTE: Commons miscategorizes this file under 'Demolished churches in Pittsburgh,' which contradicts strong, recent (2025) sourcing in our own case record confirming the building still stands as condominiums — treat the Commons 'demolished' category as a stale/incorrect tag, not a red flag on the photo's identity.

verified.verdict: accept - hero is the 2021 CC0 modern photo (clean, undistorted, current-state caption). Both CC0 modern alternates and the 1899 historic image are usable; site should NOT reuse Commons' 'Demolished churches in Pittsburgh' category as it is factually wrong per this project's own verified case record.

verified.identityEvidence: Verso caption: "St George Lithuanian, 31st and Auburn." Case-records/sv-jurgio-chicago-il.json confirms St. George, Chicago's oldest Lithuanian parish, stood at 33rd/Lituanica Ave in Bridgeport and was demolished 1990; Lituanica Avenue was renamed from Auburn Avenue on January 1, 1934 specifically to honor Lithuanian pilots who departed from this church in 1933 — so "Auburn" in the 1913 caption is simply the pre-1934 name of the same street the parish stood on. Visually a dramatic full Gothic exterior, clearly the largest/most striking of the three NBY exterior views.
